info.text: Knobology, probe movements, positioning, protocol and the common bile duct.

questiontext.text: You have just selected the abdominal preset and found the liver. Which control should you set next?

generalfeedback.text: Depth comes before gain, because changing depth changes what needs amplifying. Setting gain first means setting it twice.

questiontext.text: The far field of the liver is too dark while the near field looks correct. The right control is:

generalfeedback.text: A depth-specific problem needs a depth-specific correction. Raising overall gain would over-gain the already-adequate near field.

questiontext.text: A trainee keeps adjusting gain mid-scan and the image is still poor. The most likely real problem is:

generalfeedback.text: Once the controls are set, poor images are nearly always solved by moving the patient or the probe, not by more knob-turning.

answer.text: Windowing - position, acoustic window, or breath-hold

questiontext.text: When you increase image depth mid-study, which other control should you revisit?

generalfeedback.text: The focal zone should sit at or just deep to the region of interest; changing depth moves that region relative to the focus.

questiontext.text: Which transducer movement is responsible for covering a volume of tissue rather than a single plane?

generalfeedback.text: Fanning angles the beam through the tissue from a fixed footprint. Sliding moves you to new anatomy; it does not fill in the volume between planes.

questiontext.text: A trainee is directly observed completing the right-lobe sweep in 20 seconds, storing only one image for the region. The most likely error is:

generalfeedback.text: An observed sweep that fast, covering that little ground, is far more likely to reflect sliding than fanning. A single stored frame does not itself prove incomplete coverage, but the observed speed and technique do.

answer.text: Sliding when they should have been fanning

questiontext.text: Rotating the probe is the movement used to:

generalfeedback.text: Rotation changes the scan plane - it is how you obtain the second orthogonal view of a lesion, and how you align the footprint within an intercostal space.

answer.text: Move between transverse, sagittal and oblique scan planes

questiontext.text: Rocking (heel-toe) the probe is most useful when:

generalfeedback.text: Rocking tilts along the probe's long axis within the scan plane, improving contact and bringing a structure toward the center of the image.

answer.text: Only part of the footprint is in contact, such as over ribs
The patient cannot hold their breath

questiontext.text: Graded compression during a liver survey is used primarily to:

generalfeedback.text: Compression pushes gas out of the beam. Apply it gradually - discomfort costs you the breath-hold, which costs more than the gas did.

answer.text: Displace bowel gas and shorten the distance to the target

questiontext.text: Which position most reliably improves access to the right hepatic lobe and dome?

generalfeedback.text: Rolling the patient onto the left side brings the liver forward and downward and shifts bowel gas medially, opening the right intercostal spaces.

questiontext.text: A frail patient on a narrow couch cannot roll fully into left lateral decubitus. A reasonable alternative is:

generalfeedback.text: A partial oblique captures much of the benefit of full decubitus and is practical in outreach settings.

answer.text: Left posterior oblique, rolled about 45 degrees

questiontext.text: Sitting the patient erect during a liver study is most useful to:

generalfeedback.text: Gravity lowers the liver a few centimetres and mobilises gallbladder contents - a useful rescue maneuver.

answer.text: Drop the liver below the costal margin when subcostal views fail, and shift gallbladder contents

questiontext.text: Which instruction correctly coaches the breath-hold for a subcostal liver view?

generalfeedback.text: Deep inspiration pushes the diaphragm down and carries the liver below the costal margin.

answer.text: Take a deep breath in and hold

questiontext.text: Full inspiration sometimes worsens an intercostal view of the hepatic dome because:

generalfeedback.text: Lung brought down into the window blanks out the dome. Quiet expiration can be the better choice for that particular view.

answer.text: The liver moves out of the field entirely
Aerated lung descends into the acoustic window

questiontext.text: A patient physically cannot sustain a breath-hold. The appropriate adaptation is:

generalfeedback.text: The study can still be diagnostic; what matters is adapting technique and documenting the limitation honestly.

answer.text: Record the study as non-diagnostic and stop
Scan in short bursts at end-inspiration, accept more images and shorter sweeps, and note it in the report

questiontext.text: In the twelve-step screening protocol, repositioning the patient to left lateral decubitus should occur:

generalfeedback.text: It is a routine step. Skipping it because the first pass 'looked fine' is how dome coverage quietly goes missing.

answer.text: At the very start, before any imaging
Only if the first pass was obviously inadequate
As a routine step, re-covering anything incomplete
Never, if subcostal views were obtained

questiontext.text: Measuring splenic length during a liver screening study is worth doing because:

generalfeedback.text: It takes about twenty seconds and can strengthen a diagnosis that is equivocal from the liver alone.

answer.text: Splenomegaly is an indirect sign of portal hypertension and is often easier to see than subtle parenchymal change

questiontext.text: Storing and labeling a representative image at each protocol step primarily allows:

generalfeedback.text: A labeled image documents that a representative region was imaged. It supports, but does not by itself prove, that the entire volume was swept completely.

answer.text: Documentation that the region was imaged, reviewable by you or an over-reader later

questiontext.text: On a transverse view at the porta hepatis, the 'Mickey Mouse' arrangement consists of:

generalfeedback.text: The portal vein forms the head; the hepatic artery and CBD sit anteriorly as the ears.

answer.text: Portal vein as the head, with hepatic artery and common bile duct as the two ears
Gallbladder as the head, with cystic duct as ears
IVC as the head, with hepatic veins as ears
Aorta as the head, with renal arteries as ears

questiontext.text: Two small anechoic tubes lie anterior to the portal vein. The best way to help establish which is the duct is:

generalfeedback.text: Positive arterial flow identifies the artery. Absent color is only supportive of the duct once scale, gain, and angle have been optimized, it does not prove it on its own.

answer.text: Apply color Doppler after optimizing scale, gain, and angle - the artery fills with color, the duct does not
Measure both and take the larger

questiontext.text: The common duct is conventionally measured:

generalfeedback.text: Lumen only, longitudinal, at a consistent, defined point along its course (commonly just before it enters the pancreas), perpendicular to the long axis. Follow your local protocol's measurement convention, and distinguish this standard measurement from documentation of the widest abnormal segment if the duct is irregular.

answer.text: Only when the patient is jaundiced
Outer wall to outer wall on a transverse view
Inner wall to inner wall on a longitudinal view, at a consistent defined point along its course

questiontext.text: A conventional working upper limit for common duct diameter in an adult with the gallbladder in situ is approximately:

generalfeedback.text: Mean normal is around 4 mm; roughly 6 mm is the conventional cut-off, though published limits range between about 5 and 9 mm.

questiontext.text: A CBD of 9 mm is measured in an asymptomatic patient who had a cholecystectomy fifteen years ago. This is best interpreted as:

generalfeedback.text: Up to about 10 mm can be normal after remote cholecystectomy. Always establish the surgical history before calling a duct dilated.

answer.text: Likely physiological, since the duct enlarges progressively after cholecystectomy

questiontext.text: Biliary dilatation seen alongside a peripheral hepatic mass should shift the differential toward:

generalfeedback.text: Capsular retraction with segmental biliary obstruction is characteristic of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma rather than HCC.

questiontext.text: The distal common bile duct cannot be visualized because of duodenal gas. The correct action is:

generalfeedback.text: The distal duct is frequently obscured. Documenting that it was not seen is what keeps the report honest.

answer.text: Reposition or try erect, and if it stays hidden report the duct as incompletely visualized
Report the visualized portion as if it were the whole duct

questiontext.text: In a transverse liver column, the first probe movement after placing it high under the costal margin should be to:

generalfeedback.text: Everything above the starting point is otherwise never imaged - and that is the dome, where lesions hide.

answer.text: Fan cranially, to catch the top of the liver

questiontext.text: The liver is scanned in transverse as:

generalfeedback.text: Left, middle and right columns, each starting high with a cranial fan before descending.

answer.text: Three vertical columns worked left to right, each fanned cranially then caudally
A single sweep across the abdomen

questiontext.text: The most common error in a transverse liver sweep is:

generalfeedback.text: Starting mid-abdomen leaves everything cranial to that point unimaged.

answer.text: Starting at a comfortable mid-abdominal position and only working downward

questiontext.text: The longitudinal liver sweep is performed by:

generalfeedback.text: The rock covers craniocaudal extent at each position; the slide carries you across. One without the other leaves gaps.

answer.text: Starting on the left and gently rocking the probe up and down while sliding across to the right
Taking one sagittal image of each lobe
Fanning from a single fixed point

questiontext.text: In the longitudinal liver sweep, the rocking movement serves to:

generalfeedback.text: Sliding alone would image only one horizontal band; the rock fills in the height.

answer.text: Cover the craniocaudal extent of the liver at each position across the sweep

questiontext.text: The gallbladder should be examined in long axis by:

generalfeedback.text: A stone sitting between two static planes is a stone you did not find.

answer.text: Fanning from one wall through to the other so the entire lumen passes through the beam

questiontext.text: The transverse gallbladder examination should sweep:

generalfeedback.text: The full length must be traversed, not sampled.

answer.text: From fundus through body to neck

questiontext.text: A deep inspiration during a left lateral intercostal view of the spleen typically:

generalfeedback.text: This is the same curtain effect lung ultrasound uses deliberately. A gentle half-breath helps; a full one costs you the organ.

answer.text: Improves the image by dropping the spleen
Worsens it, because aerated lung descends across the window and obscures the spleen

questiontext.text: If the splenic image disappears as the patient breathes in, the correct instruction is:

generalfeedback.text: The lung curtain has descended across the window; less inspiration restores the view.

questiontext.text: The IVC should be imaged:

generalfeedback.text: Transverse confirms you are on the vessel and shows its shape; long axis shows course, caliber and respiratory variation.

answer.text: In both transverse and long axis

questiontext.text: When imaging the IVC in long axis to assess respiratory variation, the patient should:

generalfeedback.text: Holding the breath removes the very finding you are looking for.

answer.text: Breathe quietly, since the variation is the point

questiontext.text: The common bile duct should be assessed:

generalfeedback.text: Transverse gives the Mickey Mouse at the porta and the duct in cross-section in the pancreatic head; long axis is where you measure.

answer.text: In both transverse and long axis
In long axis only, where it is measured
Only when the patient is jaundiced

questiontext.text: Why is a transverse view of the aorta insufficient on its own?

generalfeedback.text: Both planes are needed: transverse for caliber perpendicular to the axis, long axis for the full course.

answer.text: It is only valid in thin patients
A transverse sweep can step over a focal dilatation that long axis would reveal

questiontext.text: A trainee completes the entire liver protocol in under three minutes. This raises concern chiefly about:

generalfeedback.text: A study finished this quickly raises concern about incomplete systematic coverage generally. The cranial fan at the top of each column is what most often gets skipped when a study is rushed, since it is what takes the time and covers the dome.

answer.text: The cranial fan at the top of each transverse column
